<reason>PRO read the motion correctly as a comparison among achievable long-term outcomes and forced CON's alternative (a rights-bearing single state) to meet the same "achievable" test. CON's best idea — that a rights trajectory is incremental and needs no counterparty — was genuinely strong, but PRO's "door" argument (the increments still sum to a national majority accepting minority status, and any pressure sufficient for that would buy a border more cheaply) was never squarely dismantled; CON's closing effectively conceded that "both roads run through hard Israeli politics." PRO also landed that CON's stated mechanism (let formal annexation collapse the fiction of temporariness so the world prices it) sits badly with a "least-bad" claim, and CON's denial in closing was assertion rather than answer. CON scored real hits — PRO's coalition answer ("the same kind" as Gaza) was soft, the Palestinian split went underaddressed, and "hope in the grammar of a plan" was memorable — but CON also dodged PRO's point that its own road has no falsifier. Execution costs: CON clipped twice, PRO clipped once and miscited reference IDs ([C4.4–C4.5]). Clear but competitive win for PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A4.5–A4.7 and A5.2–A5.3: turning CON's "no counterparty consent" asymmetry into the observation that equality must still be enacted or coerced through the same Jewish-Israeli majority, so CON's road runs through the same door and asks for more — with the Hebron settlers inside the shared legislature rather than outside it. CON's "different-sized asks" reply was the strongest counter but conceded the shared door.</best_rebuttal>
